reason: Crafted heartbeat requests with no login make the server return chunks of its memory, which can include private keys and session data. The leak is random and partial, so impact is limited to some of the data.
salesperson_line: Attackers can pull fragments of memory from this encrypted service, which may include private keys or session data.

reason: The scanner saw signs that an attacker already controls the host, so the attacker can use it directly with no further steps. Full control is implied by the compromise marker.
salesperson_line: Signs suggest someone outside your organisation already has control of this system and may be using it right now.

reason: The data has already been wiped or encrypted and a ransom demand left behind, so the attack is complete across the stored data. This pattern comes from active ransom campaigns against exposed databases.
salesperson_line: Your data appears to have been wiped or locked, with a ransom note left behind demanding payment to get it back.

reason: Anyone can connect and query the database without a password, so they can read, change or delete all its data. Mass ransom campaigns have repeatedly targeted open MongoDB servers.
salesperson_line: Anyone on the internet can read, change or delete the data in this database, because it asks for no password.

reason: Anyone can run commands and read keys without a password, and Redis can be made to write files that lead to code running on the server. Open Redis servers are widely mass-scanned and abused.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read and change this data store without a password, and can often use it to take over the server.

reason: The API answers with no login, so anyone can list the indices and, through the same open API, read or delete their documents. Open Elasticsearch servers are routinely wiped and held for ransom.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see and likely read or delete the data collections on this search server, because it asks for no password.

reason: Anyone can list and pull stored images without a login, and images often contain application code and embedded secrets. Public methods exist, but no widespread abuse of open registries is confirmed here.
salesperson_line: Anyone can download your stored container images, which may expose your application code and any passwords built into them.

reason: Anyone can log in as anonymous and read the files the server shares, which gives access to some data. Anonymous FTP is a well-known method, but no specific widespread campaign is reported here.
salesperson_line: Anyone can log into this file server without a password and look at some of the files stored on it.

reason: Anyone can list the share names without logging in, which reveals names rather than data. File access is not confirmed, so the lower level is chosen.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see the names of some shared folders on this Windows server without logging in, which helps plan further attacks.

reason: The server offers security type None, so anyone can open a full remote desktop with no password and control the screen and machine. Open VNC servers are widely scanned and abused.
salesperson_line: Anyone can connect to this remote desktop without a password and control the computer as if sitting at it.

reason: The device's reply includes its admin password, so no guessing is needed and anyone who asks can log in and change its settings. The disclosure itself gives full administrative control.
salesperson_line: This device hands its admin password to anyone who asks, letting them take over the device and change its settings.

reason: The admin page has no password, so anyone reaching it can change settings, which gives limited control. Browsing the page needs no special tools.
salesperson_line: Anyone can open this printer's admin page without a password and change its settings, which can help them reach your network.

reason: Anyone can send requests to the model server without login and use its compute, and some management actions can change its models. Abuse of exposed AI servers for free compute has been reported.
salesperson_line: Strangers can use this AI server for free and may be able to change the models it runs, at your expense.

reason: The control protocols answer with no login, so an attacker can read device identity and may be able to send commands, though the scan shows only identity replies. Exposed industrial systems are mass-scanned and have been targeted by hacktivists.
salesperson_line: Anyone can talk to this industrial controller over the internet and may be able to interfere with the equipment it runs.

reason: The host key is publicly known, so an attacker on the network path could impersonate the server and read or alter sessions. Without that on-path position the key alone gives no access.
salesperson_line: This server's identity key is publicly known, so someone placed between you and it could impersonate it and read sessions.

reason: The Exchange CVEs are inferred from the version and unconfirmed, but judged as real, several are pre-authentication routes to code execution. Those routes have been mass-exploited in the wild.
salesperson_line: Your Exchange mail server may have known flaws that let outsiders take it over, and these flaws are being actively attacked.

reason: The gauge answers inventory requests from the internet, revealing tank contents and levels with no login but no control. Public methods exist, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Anyone online can read this fuel system's stock levels, which could help someone plan theft or sabotage.

reason: Anyone can list the module names without logging in, which reveals folder names. File access is not confirmed, so the lower level is chosen.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see the names of some shared folders on this file-sync server without logging in, which helps further attacks.

reason: The IPMI service leaks password hashes that an attacker can take away and crack offline, but cracking needs guessing a target-specific password. Once a password is found, full control of the server's hardware follows.
salesperson_line: This server's remote management is reachable from the internet, and a weak password would give someone full control of the machine.

reason: The management service is reachable on a version with known flaws, but reaching the hypervisor usually still needs credentials or a version-specific exploit. Ransomware groups actively target exposed ESXi hosts.
salesperson_line: Your virtual server host is reachable from the internet and is a prime ransomware target, so one break-in could hit every virtual machine.

reason: The server returns recent client addresses to anyone with no login, which is information only. It can also be used to amplify attack traffic against others, and NTP amplification is actively abused.
salesperson_line: This time server lists recent visitors' addresses to anyone and can be misused to flood other systems with traffic.

reason: The server answers recursive lookups for anyone, which lets attackers use it to relay DNS amplification floods but gives no data or control of this server. Open resolvers are actively abused in DDoS attacks.
salesperson_line: Your DNS server answers lookups for anyone online, so it can be used to help flood other websites with traffic.

reason: The community string gives read access to device details, which helps later attacks but grants no control. Default community strings are mass-scanned and abused.
salesperson_line: Anyone who knows the default community string can read this device's name and details, which helps them plan attacks.

reason: The login screen gives no access by itself, but a valid login gives full desktop control, and RDP is heavily brute-forced. Guessing or stealing credentials is needed, so the attack is not automatic.
salesperson_line: Your Windows remote desktop login is open to the internet, so anyone who guesses or steals a password can take over the machine.

reason: Standard RDP Security uses weak encryption that an attacker on the network path can break to read the session. That requires an on-path position, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Remote desktop still accepts an old, weak encryption mode, so someone on your network route could read the sessions.

reason: SMBv1 is the protocol behind wormable flaws such as EternalBlue, which give full system control, but exploitation needs an unpatched flaw the scan does not confirm. Attacks on SMBv1 are widely reported.
salesperson_line: This Windows file server uses an ancient file-sharing protocol that attackers have used to take over machines at scale.

reason: Telnet asks for a username and password, so an attacker must guess or steal credentials first. Once logged in they get a full shell, and Telnet is brute-forced by IoT botnets.
salesperson_line: Anyone who guesses or steals a login can run commands on this device, and the traffic travels unencrypted.

reason: Anyone can read system metrics such as hostname, kernel and OS version, which helps later attacks but gives no control. Public methods exist, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read this server's operating system and performance details, which helps attackers choose their methods.

reason: The listing reveals file and folder names, which helps attackers find targets, but gives no control. Public methods exist, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Your web server shows a list of its files to anyone, which can reveal backups or internal files.

reason: The database answers from the internet, and a valid login would give access to all its data. Brute-force attempts on exposed databases are common, but a credential is still needed.
salesperson_line: Your database is reachable from the internet, so an attacker who guesses or steals a login could read all its data.

reason: The DICOM server accepted a connection from the internet, and it may return patient records to queries, which is partial data. Whether records are returned is not confirmed by the description.
salesperson_line: A medical imaging system accepts connections from the internet, which could expose patient information if it hands out records.

reason: Old SSLv2 and SSLv3 can be attacked to decrypt some traffic, but this needs an on-path position. Public tools exist, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: This service still accepts very old encryption, which someone on the network path could use to read some traffic.

reason: A short RSA key or MD5 or SHA1 signature weakens the certificate but gives no direct access. Breaking it is costly and needs an on-path position, and no practical public method is reported.
salesperson_line: This site's security certificate uses weak cryptography, which makes it easier for a determined attacker to impersonate it.

reason: The operating system no longer gets security patches, which leaves it exposed to future flaws, but this finding alone gives no attack path. No direct method is named.
salesperson_line: This system runs an operating system that no longer gets security updates, so newly found flaws will stay unfixed.

reason: The auth bypass lets an unauthenticated attacker retrieve the device configuration, which may contain settings and credentials but not direct control. Public exploit methods exist for these DVR and CCTV products.
salesperson_line: Attackers can download the settings file from this camera or recorder without a password, possibly including login details.

reason: An unauthenticated attacker can corrupt database files via a crafted connection, which is partial data harm. Code execution needs an authenticated user, so it is not automatic.
salesperson_line: An outsider can corrupt parts of this old database with a crafted connection, and a fuller takeover needs a login first.

reason: Heartbeat requests with no login leak chunks of server memory, which can include keys and session data. Heartbleed has been actively exploited since disclosure.
salesperson_line: Attackers can pull fragments of memory from this encrypted service, which may include private keys or session data.

reason: The FREAK downgrade needs a victim client to connect to a malicious server, so it requires tricking a user or an on-path position. Public proof-of-concept exists, with no widespread abuse reported.
salesperson_line: If staff connect to a malicious server, an attacker could weaken their encryption and read some of their traffic.

reason: Crafted HTTP requests with no login make HTTP.sys execute code, giving full system control. Exploitation of this flaw has been reported in the wild.
salesperson_line: Attackers can send a crafted web request to this Windows server and run their own code, gaining full control.

reason: Malformed headers with no login leak fragments of Jetty server memory, which gives partial data. Public proof-of-concept exists, but no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Attackers can trick this web server into leaking fragments of its memory, which may include sensitive data.

reason: The Logjam downgrade needs an on-path attacker to rewrite handshake messages, so it cannot be automated against a target alone. Public methods exist.
salesperson_line: An attacker sitting between users and this service could weaken its encryption and read some traffic.

reason: A long crafted If header in a WebDAV PROPFIND request triggers a buffer overflow that executes code on IIS 6.0. Public exploits have been used against exposed servers.
salesperson_line: This old IIS web server can be taken over by one specially crafted web request from an outsider.

reason: Unauthenticated access to the configuration file reveals device details and settings, which helps later attacks but gives no direct control. Public methods exist for these cameras.
salesperson_line: Anyone can download this camera's configuration file, which reveals its network details and settings that help attackers.

reason: A pre-authentication RDP flaw lets an attacker execute code with no login, and attacks on it have been reported. The attack needs only network reachability to the RDP port.
salesperson_line: Attackers can take over this Windows remote desktop server without a password, using a flaw that can spread between machines.

reason: A specially crafted unauthenticated URI reads arbitrary server files, which can include credentials and session keys, so impact is partial. Mass exploitation of this VPN flaw has been reported.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can read sensitive files from this VPN appliance without logging in, possibly including passwords and session keys.

reason: Command injection in the router's web interface needs administrator credentials, so it is not automatic. Once an admin is logged in, commands run as root on the router.
salesperson_line: Anyone with the router's admin login can run commands as root on it, taking complete control of the device.

reason: Requesting specific URLs with no login downloads the router configuration, which may include stored credentials. That gives partial data but not direct control.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can download this router's configuration without logging in, which may include stored login details.

reason: A crafted SMBv3 compression request with no login triggers code execution on unpatched Windows. Public proof-of-concept exists, but no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Unpatched Windows file sharing can be taken over by a specially crafted network request, with no password needed.

reason: The pre-authentication request reaches the Exchange backend with no login and is chained with related Exchange flaws to run code. Mass exploitation of ProxyLogon has been widely reported.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can reach this Exchange mail server without logging in and, using known chains, take it over completely.

reason: The insecure deserialization runs code as SYSTEM, but reaching the vulnerable service needs an earlier foothold or chained access, so it is not automatic alone. Mass exploitation of the ProxyLogon chain has been reported.
salesperson_line: Attackers who gain a foothold on this Exchange server can run code with full system control, and this flaw has been used in real attacks.

reason: The arbitrary file write needs an authenticated or chained session on Exchange, so it is not automatic alone. Once reached, planted files can lead to full control, and the chain has been mass-exploited.
salesperson_line: Once an attacker is inside this Exchange server, this flaw lets them plant files and take full control of it.

reason: The post-authentication file write needs an authenticated or chained session on Exchange, so it is not automatic alone. Once reached, it leads to code execution and full control, and the chain has been mass-exploited.
salesperson_line: Once an attacker is inside this Exchange server, this flaw lets them plant files and take full control of it.

reason: It is part of the ProxyShell chain, which allows code execution on Exchange without a login. The chain has been widely exploited in the wild.
salesperson_line: Part of a known attack chain that lets outsiders run code on this Exchange server and take it over, and this chain is being used.

reason: The security feature bypass alone gives limited access, and fuller takeover needs chaining with other Exchange flaws. It has been exploited in the wild as part of the ProxyShell chain.
salesperson_line: This Exchange flaw lets outsiders get past some security checks, and attackers combine it with others to gain deeper access.

reason: A pre-authentication path confusion bypasses access checks and reaches a code-execution route on Exchange. It has been widely exploited as part of ProxyShell.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can get past access checks on this Exchange server without logging in and run code on it, which has been exploited widely.

reason: The elevation of privilege needs an existing foothold on the Exchange server, so it is not remote on its own. Once used, it gives SYSTEM control, and it was used in ProxyShell attacks.
salesperson_line: If an attacker already has a foothold on this Exchange server, this flaw lets them gain full system control.

reason: The unauthenticated plugin path traversal reads local files, which can include config secrets and database contents, so impact is partial. Mass exploitation of Grafana was reported after disclosure.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can read files from this monitoring server without logging in, which may expose stored secrets and settings.

reason: An unauthenticated buffer overflow in the router's login CGI likely leads to code execution, giving full control of the router. Public details exist, but no confirmed widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Outsiders may be able to crash or take over this DrayTek router through its login page, without any password.

reason: Command execution needs a streaming connection the attacker can establish, which usually requires a valid API key, so it is not automatic. Commands run only as the netdata service user, giving limited control.
salesperson_line: If streaming is enabled, an outsider with the right key could run commands as the monitoring service user.

reason: The MACHINE_GUID, readable from an exposed agent, works as an API key on the parent, letting attackers read or inject monitoring data. The impact is partial access to that data.
salesperson_line: An outsider could read or inject monitoring data on this server, using identifiers readable from exposed agents.

reason: An unauthenticated request through downloader.php bypasses restrictions and executes commands on the device. Public exploit methods exist, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can run commands on this SolarView monitoring device without logging in, giving them full control of it.

reason: Spoofed reverse-proxy headers can make the server treat the request as local, allowing administrator login without a password on exposed servers. Public details exist, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Attackers can fake a header to log into this media server as an administrator without needing a password.

reason: Exposed RocketMQ components accept unauthenticated configuration updates that run commands as the RocketMQ service user, which limits impact to that user. Public exploit methods exist, and no widespread abuse is reported.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can run commands on this messaging server as its service account, which can lead to further access.

reason: The attack needs an administrator account to point the media encoder path at a network-share executable, so it is not automatic. Once admin, the attacker runs the chosen program on the server.
salesperson_line: Someone already holding an admin login on this media server could run programs of their choice on the host.

reason: Unauthenticated CLI requests read arbitrary files on the Jenkins controller, which can expose stored secrets and credentials, so impact is partial. Mass exploitation of this flaw has been widely reported.
salesperson_line: Outsiders can read files from this Jenkins server without logging in, which may expose stored passwords and keys.

reason: Crafted requests with no login make the NetScaler gateway leak memory, which can include active session tokens, so impact is partial. Exploitation in the wild has been reported.
salesperson_line: Attackers can pull memory from this VPN gateway without logging in, potentially stealing active user sessions.

reason: Crafted HTTP requests with no login make HTTP.sys execute code on Windows servers, giving full control. Exploitation has been reported in the wild.
salesperson_line: Attackers can send a crafted web request to this Windows server and run their own code, gaining full control.

reason: Crafted SMBv1 messages with no login execute code on unpatched Windows, and this flaw family was used in worm-like ransomware outbreaks. It gives full system control.
salesperson_line: Unpatched Windows file sharing lets attackers run their own code with no login, the flaw behind major ransomware outbreaks.
